candidates.source_name: Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle)
candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 16:3 (Abraham cycle (16:3)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And we announced to Sarah all that the angel had told us, and they both rejoiced with exceeding great joy' — the angel of presence reports the Isaac-birth annunciation to Sarah. Jubilees frames this as a formal annunciation-to-the-matriarch parallel to Mary's annunciation. The Tewahedo Marian-typology tradition (Wǝddase Maryam, Mälk'ǝa Maryam) draws on Sarah's annunciation as the canonical OT type: same angelic agent (the angel of presence corresponds to Gabriel in later identification), same response (joy), same miraculous-conception substance. The Tewahedo distinctive Marian liturgical depth has its OT-typological roots here.

candidates.source_name: Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle)
candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 16:13 (Abraham cycle (16:13)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the middle of the sixth month the Lord visited Sarah and did unto her as He had spoken, and she conceived. And she bare a son in the third month, and in the middle of the month, on the day that the Lord had spoken to Abraham, on the festival of the first-fruits of the harvest, Isaac was born' — Jubilees dates Isaac's birth precisely to Shavuot (the Feast of First-Fruits / Weeks). The Tewahedo Pentecost preserves the Old-and-New-Covenant double commemoration: Isaac's birth (the promised seed) and the Spirit's descent (Acts 2, the promised Paraclete) on the same calendar date. Tewahedo Pentecost vigil chants explicitly invoke both.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And he built there an altar to the Lord who had delivered him, and who was making him rejoice in the land of his sojourning, and he celebrated a festival of joy in this month seven days' — Abraham celebrates the FIRST Feast of Tabernacles, seven days, at the Beersheba altar, the year of Isaac's birth (Jub 16:20-25). Tewahedo Sukkot (Mäskäl-related joy-week) draws canonical warrant: the seven-day festival was instituted by Abraham PRE-Mosaically, not at Lev 23. This parallels Jub 6:17's pre-Mosaic Feast of Weeks: Tewahedo liturgical pattern is that the great festivals are patriarchal restorations, not Mosaic novelties — Christ's coming brings them to fulfilment, but they pre-exist.

'And it is written on the heavenly tablets concerning Israel that they shall celebrate the feast of tabernacles seven days with joy, in the seventh month, acceptable before the Lord — a statute forever throughout their generations every year' — Jubilees confirms the heavenly-tablet inscription of the seven-day Tabernacles festival. Tewahedo liturgical historiography distinguishes festivals 'on the heavenly tablets' (pre-existent in the divine eternity, revealed through canonical Scripture) from merely-ecclesiastical commemorations: Tabernacles, Weeks, Atonement, Sabbath are in the former class. The seven-day duration is preserved in Tewahedo Mäskäl-week observance.

Tewahedo liturgical historiography distinguishes festivals 'on the heavenly tablets' (pre-existent in the divine eternity, revealed through canonical Scripture) from merely-ecclesiastical commemorations: Tabernacles, Weeks, Atonement, Sabbath are in the former class. The seven-day duration is preserved in Tewahedo Mäskäl-week observance.
